title: Anti Forensics
summary: Anti-forensics is the set of techniques an adversary uses to frustrate, mislead or delay forensic analysis, either by destroying evidence, by making analysis uneconomic, or by planting artefacts that send investigators down the wrong path. The category spans data destruction such as secure wiping, free-space overwriting and the deletion of logs; artefact manipulation including timestamp alteration, log tampering and the removal of entries from event or audit trails; concealment through encryption, steganography, alternate data streams, hidden partitions and packed or obfuscated binaries; tool subversion, where malicious code interferes with the very utilities a responder would run, including kernel-mode rootkits and the disabling of security logging; and attribution attacks such as the deliberate use of another organisation's naming conventions or living-off-the-land binaries to blend into normal activity. For defenders, anti-forensics matters less as a list of tools than as an interpretive warning: the absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, and the failure of a standard tool to find something may itself be a finding worth pursuing. Investigations respond by collecting volatile data before artefacts can be altered, corroborating every conclusion across independent sources, validating acquisition and analysis tools against known-good behaviour, and treating inconsistencies in timestamps or log continuity as investigative leads. Reporting anti-forensic indicators, including gaps, tampering and tool anomalies, alongside substantive findings protects the credibility of the case and informs detection engineering, because these techniques often require behaviour that can be detected even when the artefacts themselves cannot be recovered.
objectives: Categorise anti-forensic techniques by whether they destroy, manipulate, conceal or misattribute evidence.
Interpret missing, discontinuous or inconsistent artefacts as investigative findings rather than as proof of innocence.
Adapt collection order and tooling when an environment may contain kernel-level or tool-subverting implants.
Corroborate conclusions across independent evidence sources so they withstand deliberate artefact manipulation.
Map observed anti-forensic behaviour to adversary tactics and identify the detection opportunities it creates.
Document and communicate confidence limits when evidence integrity or completeness is in question.
Brief stakeholders on how anti-forensics affects scope estimates, investigation timelines and legal defensibility.

beginner.definition: Anti-forensics is the set of tricks an attacker uses to confuse, delay, or mislead an investigation. Some tricks destroy evidence, such as wiping files or clearing logs. Others hide evidence using encryption or hidden storage. Others plant false clues. If you investigate incidents, anti-forensics tells you when to trust your tools.
beginner.whyItMatters: When evidence is missing, it is easy to assume nothing happened. That is a dangerous mistake. Anti-forensics means the absence of evidence is not proof of innocence. An attacker who deletes logs, changes file times, or hides code can make a clean-looking machine hide a real break-in. If you ignore this, you may close an incident that is still active.
howItWorks: The attacker gains access and then works to slow down anyone who investigates later.
They destroy evidence, for example by wiping free disk space or deleting security logs.
They hide evidence by encrypting files, using hidden storage areas, or packing programs so tools cannot read them.
They change file times and log entries so your timeline no longer matches what really happened.
They may also break the tools you rely on, so your own software reports nothing suspicious.
You respond by collecting fragile evidence first and checking every finding against a second source.
beginner.example: Think of a burglar who breaks into a house, then tidies up before leaving. The chairs sit straight, the dishes are washed, and the door is locked again. Nothing looks wrong, so you assume nobody came in. Then you notice the clock on the wall shows the wrong time and the garden gate is open. Anti-forensics works the same way. The missing signs and the strange details are your real clues.
takeaways: Missing evidence is itself a clue, never proof that nothing happened.
Collect fragile data early, before an attacker or a reboot removes it.
Always confirm important findings with a second and independent evidence source.

exercises.title: Anti Forensics - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: Anti Forensics - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: Anti Forensics - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.
